content: Etravirine is a medication used in combination with other antiretroviral drugs to manage HIV infection. It works by reducing the amount of HIV in the body, thereby improving the function of the immune system. This helps lower the risk of developing HIV-related complications, such as opportunistic infections or certain cancers, and enhances overall quality of life. However, it is not a cure for HIV. This medication is typically prescribed to individuals who have previously used other HIV medications, such as efavirenz, nevirapine, or delavirdine, which were not effective enough in controlling their HIV. Etravirine belongs to a class of drugs known as non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). To minimize the risk of transmitting HIV to others, it is essential to continue taking all HIV medications exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Additionally, use effective barrier methods, such as latex or polyurethane condoms or dental dams, during sexual activity as directed by your healthcare provider. Avoid sharing personal items like needles, syringes, toothbrushes, or razors that may come into contact with blood or bodily fluids. Before starting etravirine, read the patient information leaflet provided by your pharmacist. Take this medication orally after a meal, as directed by your doctor, usually twice daily. Swallow the tablets whole. If you have difficulty swallowing, you may dissolve the tablet in a small amount of water (about 1 teaspoon or 5 milliliters). Stir the mixture well until it appears milky, then add more water, orange juice, or milk (about 1 tablespoon or 15 milliliters) and drink it immediately. Rinse the glass with additional liquid and drink it to ensure the entire dose is consumed. Repeat rinsing and drinking several times to ensure no medication is left behind. It is crucial to take this medication, along with other HIV medications, exactly as prescribed. Do not increase, decrease, or skip doses without consulting your doctor. For optimal effectiveness, take the medication at evenly spaced intervals. If you miss a dose, take it after a meal as soon as you remember. If it has been more than six hours since the missed dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regular time. Store etravirine in its original bottle at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the desiccant (drying agent) in the bottle and ensure the bottle is tightly closed when not in use. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Etravirine may interact with other medications, including other HIV drugs, macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin, clarithromycin), and rifamycins (e.g., rifabutin, rifampin, rifapentine). These interactions can affect how etravirine or the other medications work. Inform your doctor and pharmacist about all the products you use, including prescription, non-prescription, and herbal products. Your doctor may need to adjust your treatment or monitor you more closely if you are taking certain combinations of HIV medications. Common side effects of etravirine include nausea and mild rash, which usually occurs during the second week of treatment and resolves within 1 to 2 weeks. However, it is important to distinguish this from a rare rash that may indicate a severe allergic reaction. Notify your doctor immediately if you experience symptoms of a serious allergic reaction, such as severe rash, itching/swelling, dizziness, or trouble breathing. As your immune system strengthens, it may begin to fight off previously hidden infections, potentially causing symptoms of these infections to reappear. In some cases, the immune system may become overactive, leading to symptoms of inflammation. These reactions can occur at any time during treatment, even months after starting HIV therapy. Changes in body fat distribution may occur while taking this medication, such as increased fat in the upper back and stomach areas and decreased fat in the arms and legs. The cause and long-term effects of these changes are not fully understood. If someone overdoses on etravirine and exhibits severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services (911 in the U.S.) immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Regular medical and laboratory tests, such as viral load and T-cell counts, are necessary while taking this medication to monitor your progress and detect any side effects. Keep all medical and lab appointments as scheduled. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about etravirine. It does not guarantee that the medication is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
